name: Question 5
problem: Consider a spherical rocky planet with radius $(5.8\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g=7.5\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Which differential equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the rocky planet, where $r$ is the distance from the rocky planet's center to the object? Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
worked_solution:
According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the rocky planet is

$$
{F}_{\text{in}}=G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the rocky planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-{F}_{\text{in}}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance,

$$
a=-\frac{k}{{r}^{2}},
$$

with constant of proportionality $k=GM>0.$

When at the surface, $r=(5.8\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m},$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-7.5\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-7.5 & =-\frac{k}{(5.8\times {10}^{4})^{2}} \\ k & =7.5\cdot (5.8\times {10}^{4})^{2} \\  & =7.5\cdot (5.8)^{2}\times ({10}^{4})^{2} \\  & =252.3\times {10}^{8} \\  & =2.523\times {10}^{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a=-\frac{2.523\times {10}^{10}}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\frac{dv}{dr}=-\frac{2.523\times {10}^{10}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

Question 5
?

Consider a spherical rocky planet with radius (5.8×104)m and surface gravitational acceleration g=7.5m/s2. Which differential equation best models the velocity v of an object projected radially outward from the rocky planet, where r is the distance from the rocky planet's center to the object? Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.

a
vdvdr=−2.523×1010r2
b
dvdr=−2.400×1010r2
c
dvdr=−2.523×1010r2
d
vdvdr=−2.700×1010r2
e
vdvdr=−2.400×1010r2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the rocky planet is

Fin=GmMr2,

where G is the gravitational constant, m is the object's mass, and M is the rocky planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking outward as positive, is F=−Fin. Applying Newton's second law, F=ma, where a is the acceleration of the object, we have

F=−Finma=−GmMr2a=−GMr2.

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, a=−kr2, with constant of proportionality k=GM>0.

When at the surface, r=(5.8×104)m, the acceleration of the object due to gravity is a=−7.5m/s2. Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for k:

−7.5=−k(5.8×104)2k=7.5⋅(5.8×104)2=7.5⋅(5.8)2×(104)2=252.3×108=2.523×1010

Substituting back into the equation, we get

a=−2.523×1010r2.

Finally, since acceleration a is the derivative of velocity v, which is the derivative of distance r, we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating v as a function of r along the trajectory:

a=dvdt=drdt⋅dvdr=vdvdr

Therefore, substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

vdvdr=−2.523×1010r2
